newsitem.title: USA: IMF's Mussa says U.K. monetary policy appropriate.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Mussa says U.K. monetary policy appropriate.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official Wednesday called the current stance of U.K. monetary policy appropriate but suggested that interest rates may have to rise next year if economic growth picks up.
"As for the current situation, I think our assessment would be that monetary policy is appropriate," IMF chief economist Michael Mussa told a news conference.

Inflation is expected to drop below the authorities' 2-1/2 percent ceiling by early 1997. But Mussa saw a risk that it could pick up again later if U.K. economic growth strengthens, as the IMF expects.
"If the pick-up in growth materializes as we expect, then our anticipation would be ... some modest monetary firming would be needed," Mussa said.

In its semi-annual World Economic Outlook, the IMF sees U.K. growth picking up to three percent in 1997, from 2.2 percent in 1996. Retail prices, excluding mortgage interest, are expected to rise 2.4 percent in 1997 after advancing 2.7 percent this year.
"There may still be some room for some further reduction (in unemployment) without undue inflationary risks," the IMF added.
The IMF is also advocating some modest tightening of British fiscal policy.
It warned Britain against cutting taxes sharply before the next general election and said the country instead needed to take action to bring public borrowing back on track.
The IMF said financial markets already appear concerned over the budget outlook and could be upset further if taxes were slashed.

"There is some risk ... that financial market confidence and long-term interest rates ... could be more adversely affected by continuing fiscal slippage, especially if the authorities were to introduce significant tax cuts before the next general election," the IMF said.
"Corrective measures are needed to put the public finances back on track toward the authorities' goal of balance over the medium term," it added.
The Fund though was generally upbeat about the outlook for the British economy, forecasting faster growth and lower inflation next year.
